Port Alder ferries to run later on Fridays

By Mia Chen, October 19, 2026

Port Alder's harbour ferries will sail an hour later on Friday and Saturday nights from 6 November, the transit board decided on Monday, after a summer trial in which the last scheduled sailing left half empty and the added late one filled both ways.

The last crossing from the Quay terminal will leave at 12:15 a.m. instead of 11:15 p.m., and the last return from Fennel Point at 12:45 a.m. Weekday timetables do not change, and the Sunday service keeps its two-hour gaps until the new vessel is delivered in spring.

Board chair Imogen Hale said the trial was meant to answer a simple question: whether people would use a late boat if one existed. About 1,900 passengers rode the extra sailings across twelve weekends, roughly four times what the operator had planned for.

Fares stay where they are. An adult single is still $4.50, a youth single $2.25, and the monthly pass $96, which the board said it has no plan to raise before the next review in 2028. Cash is accepted on board only on the daytime boats.

Local businesses had pressed for the change. The owner of a Fennel Point bakery, Tomas Reyes, told the board that his evening staff had been taking taxis around the harbour at their own expense because the last boat left before his kitchen closed.

Not everyone was persuaded. A residents' group on the Quay side argued that late sailings would bring noise to the terminal at night, and asked for a review of the horn schedule. The board agreed to measure sound levels during the first month.

The operator, Alder Harbour Ferries, will add two deckhands to the late roster and move one mechanic to evenings. Its general manager said the cost was about $140,000 a year, less than the extra fare revenue seen in the trial if ridership holds.

Some local sites ask readers to "subscribe to continue reading" after two stories; the council said it would not do the same with its service notices, which stay free on its own website and at every terminal noticeboard.

Parking at the Quay terminal will stay free until 9 p.m. and cost $3 flat after that, a change from the trial, when it was free all night. The board said the fee covers the overnight attendant and that the lot at Fennel Point remains free at all hours.

Cyclists can board without a ticket on the two late sailings, a perk that the board extended from the summer. Bikes are limited to twelve a crossing, and the deckhands will turn the thirteenth away rather than delay the departure.

The board also approved a pilot of text-message alerts for cancellations. Passengers can register a phone number at either terminal or on the operator's website; the service is free and the numbers are deleted after the pilot ends in March.

Accessibility upgrades are on a separate track. The Quay ramp will be regraded in January, during which the terminal will be served by a temporary platform, and the Fennel Point lift, out since August, is expected back before the first late sailing.

Asked about the weather, the operator said the late boats follow the same rules as the day ones: a crossing is cancelled when winds at the harbour mouth pass 55 kilometres an hour, and the board's alerts will say so before the boat is due.

The vessel due in spring, the MV Heron, carries 220 passengers against the 140 of the boats now in service, and has a covered upper deck, a ramp for wheelchairs at both ends and space for twenty bicycles. Its builder has promised delivery by the end of April.

Ridership has been climbing for three years. The operator counted 1.4 million crossings last year, up from 1.1 million, and expects the later boats and the larger vessel to carry it past two million by 2029, the figure at which the board has promised to revisit fares.

The ferry line is older than the city's bridge. It began in 1911 with a single steam launch and a boatman who rang a bell from the Quay steps, and the present timetable still keeps the 7:05 a.m. departure that the launch made when it carried the harbour's bakers to work.

Safety statistics were presented alongside the vote. The operator reported no passenger injuries on the late sailings and two minor incidents on the day boats, both involving slippery boarding steps, which have since been fitted with a rubber tread.

Environmental groups welcomed the new vessel but asked the board to consider an electric drive. The operator said a battery conversion of the current boats would cost about $3 million each and would be examined as part of the 2028 review.

On the council floor, one member asked whether the money would be better spent on a second bridge crossing. The chair replied that the bridge study was a separate matter and had been before the council for six years without a funding source.

Tourism officials said the later boats open an option they had long lacked: an evening harbour dinner that does not end with a taxi. Two restaurants at Fennel Point have already announced late seatings on Fridays starting in November.

A trial of a seasonal Sunday evening service, which would add one return trip between six and eight p.m., was proposed by a board member but deferred to the spring after the new vessel arrives and the operator has staff to cover it.

The new timetable takes effect on Friday 6 November. Printed copies will be at both terminals from the last week of October, and the full schedule is already on the operator's website for anyone planning ahead.
